clue.text: Cynical old tub-thumper

parts.note: an ancient Greek philosopher of the Cynic school who, legend says, lived in a tub or barrel and preached loudly

explanation.surface: A jaded veteran rabble-rouser banging on about the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tub-thumper' usually means a ranting orator; here it is literal: the Cynic philosopher famously lived in a large tub, and Cynical takes a capital-C sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The founder figure of Cynic philosophy is reputed to have slept in a storage jar in Athens.

clue.text: Junior's first and last seen as a villain here in Texas

definitions.text: Junior's first and last seen as a villain here in Texas

parts.words: Junior's first and last seen as a villain here in Texas
parts.note: J.R. Ewing, known as Junior, was the scheming villain of a long-running TV soap named after a Texas city

explanation.surface: A Texan junior first and last appearing as a baddie.
explanation.walkthrough: Junior is J.R. Ewing, the villain of the TV soap set in this Texas city, where he was seen from the first episode to the last.
explanation.definitionFit: The Texan city gave its name to the soap opera in which J.R. Ewing was the archetypal villain.

clue.text: Radios can corrupt the islanders

indicators.note: to corrupt something is to spoil its proper form, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that broadcasting is spoiling island folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupt' tells you to rearrange RADIOS CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the Orkney Islands, off the north of Scotland, are known by this name.

clue.text: Demanded payment of small account in from Edward

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for account inside the other two pieces

parts.note: ex is Latin for from, as in ex-works
Ted is a pet form of the name Edward
AC is a short form of account

explanation.surface: A man named Edward is asked to pay a small bill.
explanation.walkthrough: EX (from) and TED (Edward) are joined, and 'in' puts AC (account, abbreviated) between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To have extracted money as a debt is to have insisted on and collected it.

clue.text: Presbyterian type of statesman?

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of politician a Presbyterian makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay official governing a Presbyterian church holds this title, and a senior respected politician is called this kind of statesman.

clue.text: The demon drink? Take it away

explanation.surface: A temperance warning: alcohol is the devil, so remove the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Distilled liquor is called by this word, and to whisk something off secretly is to do this to it, usually followed by 'away'.

clue.text: Pet dogs take the party up in icy regions

indicators.note: in places the turned word for a party within the regions

parts.note: the North and South Poles are the frozen ends of the earth

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Pet dogs are taken on an upbeat party at the poles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the party word, as this is a down clue, and 'in' sets it within the icy regions. 'Pet dogs' reads like a verb phrase but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: These curly-coated dogs are a familiar breed of pet.

clue.text: Sort of day for staying in, there's little hope outside

indicators.note: outside says the hope word wraps around the other piece

parts.note: a ray of hope is a small glimmer of it

explanation.surface: A gloomy day for staying indoors, with not much optimism outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps the little hope around 'in'; 'for staying' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet day, with showers falling, is the type you spend indoors.

clue.text: Factory that gives us everything!

explanation.surface: Praise for a plant that supplies us with all we want.
explanation.definitionFit: An industrial plant is called a works, and 'the whole lot' is an informal sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Only one of two white balls is so clean

definitions.text: Only one of two white balls is so

explanation.surface: Of the two white balls, only one is pristine.
explanation.walkthrough: In billiards the two white cue balls are told apart by a black dot on one; the other, unmarked, is the 'plain' ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A billiard cue ball with no dot is unmarked, and anything immaculate is likewise free of marks.

clue.text: A result of letting new maid clean or skip her work?

definitions.text: A result of letting new maid clean or skip her work?

parts.words: A result of letting new maid clean or skip her work
parts.note: a hurried, perfunctory wash or tidy, the sort of slapdash job a new servant might do while vowing to do better later

explanation.surface: A householder wondering what happens when an untrained maid either half-cleans or skips the chores.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a British idiom for a quick, superficial clean, with a vow of a proper job later; the clue pictures a lazy maid giving exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a cursory wash or clean, a token swipe now with a pledge to finish properly later.

clue.text: No cooking can satisfy him

parts.note: cooking the books means falsifying accounts, and an inspector of accounts will never be satisfied by that

explanation.surface: A fussy diner whom no chef can please.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a picky eater; 'cooking' means fiddling the accounts, which a checker of company books exists to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: An accounts inspector examines a firm's books, so any doctored figures would fail his scrutiny.

clue.text: What's said to indicate the huntsman's view?

definitions.text: What's said to indicate the huntsman's view?

parts.words: What's said to indicate the huntsman's view
parts.note: the traditional cry a fox-hunter gives on sighting the quarry

explanation.surface: Someone asking what words express a hunter's opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'View' looks like opinion, but in fox hunting it means sighting the fox, which the huntsman announces with a set cry.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the shout of British fox hunting raised when a rider first spots the fox.

clue.text: Ambled in casually for one of those jaws …

indicators.note: done casually, without care, so the letters of the two words are loosely reworked

explanation.surface: Someone strolled in nonchalantly, and the ellipsis promises more about jaws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casually' tells you to rearrange AMBLED IN. The ellipsis links to the next clue, whose answer has famous jaws.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the anatomical term for a jawbone, especially the lower one.

clue.text: Dangler to ring for service

parts.note: a cord hanging in a belfry that is pulled to sound the church bell, calling people to a service

explanation.surface: A hanging cord pulled to summon a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' suggests calling a servant, but it is also a church service, rung in by pulling this cord in a belfry.
explanation.definitionFit: This hanging cord is pulled to ring a bell, in a church tower or a big house.

clue.text: … the danger, we read, of this

definitions.text: the danger, we read, of this

parts.words: the danger, we read, of this
parts.note: continuing the previous clue: the novel Jaws is about the peril posed by a great sea predator

explanation.surface: Following on from jaws: we read about the menace of this creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with the previous clue: 'those jaws … the danger, we read, of this' points to Peter Benchley's novel Jaws, about a great white.
explanation.definitionFit: The predatory fish in the bestselling novel Jaws terrorises a seaside resort.

clue.text: Starter with a gun ?

parts.note: not a race official with a pistol, but someone who starts a fight, weapon in hand

explanation.surface: The official who fires a pistol to start a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The starter of a race fires a gun; here the starter is the one who begins hostilities.
explanation.definitionFit: The party who attacks first, starting a conflict, is so called.

clue.text: Winner gets home at the end of it?

definitions.text: Winner gets home at the end of it?

parts.words: Winner gets home at the end of it
parts.note: a horse race over ground with no jumps, where the first past the finishing post wins

explanation.surface: A competitor who goes home after the event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets home' is racing slang for winning by reaching the finish, the 'home' of a race run on level turf with no fences.
explanation.definitionFit: This horse race is run on level turf without hurdles or fences.

clue.text: Radiation device for a loafer, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word for a loafer is to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a lazer is someone who lazes about, an idler

explanation.surface: Someone choosing a beam device for an idle person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loafer' is not a shoe here: one who lazes is a 'lazer', which sounds like the light-beam device.
explanation.definitionFit: This device emits a narrow, intense beam of light, a form of electromagnetic radiation.

clue.text: Beginnings of repentance the Walrus showed

definitions.text: Beginnings of repentance the Walrus showed

parts.note: the first two letters of the word repentance
morse is an old word for a walrus

explanation.surface: Lewis Carroll's walrus showing the first signs of being sorry for eating the oysters.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's poem the Walrus weeps over the oysters he eats, so the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep regret for wrongdoing is the feeling the weeping Walrus showed.

clue.text: Lots of strikes

explanation.surface: A period of widespread industrial action.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty of something is a generous helping, as in heaps of cream; and blows from a whip are also called this.

clue.text: Cross-eyed awareness ?

parts.note: cross-eyed eyes turn inward, so their seeing is directed in, a pun on perception of one's own mind

explanation.surface: Asking what a squinting person perceives.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross-eyed eyes point inwards, so their vision is literally 'in-sight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep understanding of a person or situation is perception that looks within.

clue.text: Others the accountant includes in the run-down

indicators.note: includes means the accountant's letters hold the other piece

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant
the rest means the others

explanation.surface: An accountant's summary takes in everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' sets the others inside the accountant. The Cresta Run is the famous ice toboggan run at St Moritz, Switzerland, so 'run-down' is a run you go down.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous ice chute at St Moritz is a run that tobogganists go down head first.

clue.text: Bray's vicar in better shape

explanation.surface: A country parson who has got fitter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, in an old English song, changed his religion with each monarch to keep his living: the type of a political turncoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A time-server who shifts allegiance with the wind is so called, and a neater, fitter thing is in better trim.

clue.text: Stress is cut somehow at a stroke

indicators.note: somehow means in some way or other, so the letters are arranged in some other order

explanation.surface: Stress is relieved in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' tells you to rearrange IS CUT. 'at a stroke' adds a second hint: the word also means a beat or stroke in metre and medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody this is the rhythmic accent falling on a syllable.

clue.text: Stick with the old city chemist

parts.note: to stick paper up is to glue or paste it
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: Someone holding on to the ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Pasteur was the French chemist who developed pasteurisation and vaccines.

clue.text: The tea-girl gets the bird

explanation.surface: The girl who makes the tea is given a parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, 'Polly put the kettle on' so that everyone can have tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme girl puts the kettle on for tea, and the name is the stock name for a pet parrot.

clue.text: Proper students of Pope?

parts.note: Alexander Pope wrote that the proper study of mankind is man, so those who study humankind are his proper students

explanation.surface: Earnest scholars of the pontiff or of the poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope is the poet Alexander Pope, not the pontiff: his Essay on Man says 'the proper study of mankind is man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scientists of humankind and its cultures pursue exactly the study Pope called proper.

clue.text: Lent no more for this Pacific island

explanation.surface: A Pacific island where the fasting season is over.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian festival ends the forty-day fast, and the remote island of giant stone heads in the South Pacific bears its name.

clue.text: Emotional outbreak this year

indicators.note: an outbreak lets the letters break out of their order, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A news report of a wave of emotional frenzy over the past twelve months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outbreak' tells you to rearrange THIS YEAR, while the whole clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncontrolled, excessive emotion breaking out in a person or crowd is called by this word.
